source_text: Ergo superbia illa, quae volebat otiari, et desidiam suam ob id colore necessitatis obnubere, ut in susceptione Gentium reclamaret Evangelio; audit quoniam etsi sic esset quomodo tu commentaris, tamen supplicare Deo, non seditionem excitare deberes; quibus verbis nequitiam retundit hominis, qui diversitatem meritorum ex voluntatis qualitate venientem, aucupans elocutionis ambiguum, ideo necessitati divinae conabatur adscribere, ut assereret necesse esse alterum de duobus, id est, aut Gentes ad promissionis non venire consortium aut, si hoc liceret Deo, exstingui officia liberae voluntatis. Verum quia id non sufficiebat negotio; neque enim a tali magistro, sicut commendabatur auctoritas Dei, ita erat indefensa relinquenda iustitia; subdit consequentissime vasa, quae in contumelia et quae in honore fiunt, habere hoc de propriae stipendio voluntatis. Si enim Deus volens ostendere iram, et notam facere potentiam suam in multa patientia, in vasis irae, consummatis in perditionem; et ut notas faceret, inquit, divitias gloriae suae in vasis misericordiae, quae praeparavit in gloriam, quos et vocavit nos, non solum ex Iudaeis, sed etiam ex Gentibus [n360] . Certe hic absolvit, quod superior conflictus operuerat, non inferri a Deo iram nisi his vasis, quae ad perditionem consummata fuerint; gloriam autem dari his, quae ad hoc fuerint praeparata. A quo autem vasa huiusmodi in susceptionem horum quae diximus praeparentur, ipsius Apostoli sermo patefecit. In magna, inquit, domo, non sunt tantummodo vasa aurea et argentea, sed et lignea et fictilia; alia quidem in honorem, alia in contumeliam. Si ergo mundaverit quis semetipsum ab his, erit vas in honorem sanctificatum, utile Domino, ad omne opus bonum paratum [n361] .
pass_a_gloss: Therefore that pride, which was wanting to be idle, and to cloud its own sloth on account of this with a color of necessity, that in the taking-up of the Nations it would cry against the Gospel; hears that even if it were so as you comment, nevertheless you ought to supplicate God, not to stir a sedition; by which words he beats back the wickedness of a human, who the diversity of deserts coming from the quality of will, hunting an ambiguous expression, was therefore trying to ascribe to a divine necessity, that he would assert it necessary that one of two, that is, either the Nations not come to the consortium of the promise or, if this were allowed to God, the offices of free will be extinguished. But because that was not sufficing for the business; for neither by such a teacher, as the authority of God was being commended, so was justice to be left undefended; he subjects most consequently that the vessels, which are made unto insult and which unto honor, have this from the stipend of their own will. For if God willing to show wrath, and to make known his power in much patience, in vessels of wrath, consummated unto perdition; and that he might make known, he says, the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, which he prepared unto glory, whom he also called us, not only from the Jews, but also from the Nations. Certainly here he absolves, what the upper conflict had covered, that wrath is not brought by God except to these vessels, which shall have been consummated unto perdition; but glory is given to these, which shall have been prepared unto this. But by whom vessels of this kind are prepared into the taking-up of these things which we have said, the speech of the Apostle himself made open. In a great house, he says, there are not only gold and silver vessels, but also wooden and earthen; some indeed unto honor, others unto insult. If therefore anyone shall have cleansed himself from these, he will be a vessel unto honor sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared unto every good work.

pass_b_english: That pride wished to remain idle and cover its laziness with an appearance of necessity, so as to protest against the Gospel's reception of the nations. It therefore hears: “Even if matters were as you imagine, you should nevertheless petition God, not stir up a revolt.” With these words Paul checks the man's wickedness. Seizing upon ambiguous language, that man tried to attribute to divine necessity the difference in deserts that comes from the character of the will. He wanted to establish that one of two things must follow: either the nations do not enter into fellowship in the promise, or, if God is permitted to admit them, the tasks of free will are abolished.

But this did not suffice for the issue. Such a teacher could not commend God's authority while leaving his justice undefended. Most consistently, then, Paul adds that vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the wages of their own will: “If God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known with great patience in vessels of wrath completed for destruction, and to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory, whom he also called, namely us, not only from Jews but also from the nations” (Romans 9:22–24). Here he certainly clears up what the previous debate had concealed: God brings wrath only upon vessels completed for destruction, while glory is given to those prepared for it. By whom such vessels are prepared to receive the things we have named, the apostle's own words disclose: “In a great house there are not only gold and silver vessels but also wooden and earthenware ones, some for honor and some for dishonor. If, then, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:20–21).
